topic: Observer effect on a directly timed baseline
stem: A team establishes a handling-time baseline by sitting with case handlers and timing their work. What is the main threat to that measurement, and the standard mitigation?

options.text: Sample size is too small; mitigate by extending the timing exercise across a full quarter of production casework.
People work differently when watched, usually faster and more by the book; mitigate by triangulating against system measures.
Observers' clocks drift apart; mitigate by issuing one shared stopwatch application to everyone taking measurements on the floor.
Handlers may refuse to take part; mitigate by making participation in the timing study mandatory across the whole team.

explanation.correct: Observation changes the thing observed, and it biases in a predictable direction: fewer interruptions taken, shortcuts avoided, the documented procedure followed more closely than usual. A baseline inflated by good behaviour understates the current cost and therefore understates the improvement the system delivers — which is the wrong direction for a business case that will be challenged later. Cross-checking against timestamps or throughput the system already records, and letting the novelty wear off over several days, brings the estimate back toward normal working.

distractors.A: More observation of a biased measure produces a more precise biased measure. Duration helps only insofar as behaviour reverts to normal, which is part of the real mitigation rather than a fix in itself.
distractors.C: A trivial mechanical concern next to the behavioural one. Seconds of clock difference are irrelevant when the activity being timed varies by minutes according to who is watching.
distractors.D: Compelling participation may raise coverage but sharpens the observation effect, since handlers who feel monitored under instruction perform even more carefully. It also damages the relationship with the team whose cooperation the project needs.

explanation.concept: Every baseline instrument carries a bias, and the job is to name it and offset it. Direct observation biases toward best behaviour, self-reporting toward round numbers and forgotten interruptions, and system timestamps toward including waiting time. Use at least two instruments and treat the disagreement between them as information rather than noise.
explanation.tip: Baseline questions usually hinge on which direction the bias runs. Ask whether the measurement makes today's process look better or worse than it is, and remember that a flattering baseline shrinks your own benefit.

topic: Qualifying a low-volume, high-consequence use case
stem: A nuclear decommissioning contractor asks for Claude to draft radiological protection assessments. There are about thirty a year; each takes a qualified specialist roughly three weeks; there are four such specialists and one retires within twelve months. Every assessment is independently checked by a second specialist and approved by the site regulator's inspector. What should qualification conclude?

options.text: Decline: thirty assessments a year cannot justify the build cost, and no evaluation set of usable size can be assembled from that volume.
Accept with specialist weeks saved per assessment as the success criterion, since three weeks per item is a very large per-unit gain.
Accept, targeting fully automated drafting of the whole assessment so the capacity lost when the fourth specialist retires is directly replaced.
Accept, framing the value as retained capacity and captured expertise, with acceptance by expert review against historical assessments.

explanation.correct: Low volume changes what the value is and how it can be measured, not whether the case qualifies. The scarce resource is four specialists shrinking to three, so the benefit is capacity preservation and the encoding of expertise that is about to walk out of the building — not a throughput number. Measurement has to adapt too: with thirty cases a year no threshold can be estimated with confidence, so acceptance rests on expert comparison of drafts against completed historical assessments, which the contractor already holds in quantity.

distractors.A: Applies a volume heuristic to a case where the per-item stake is enormous and the driver is a capability cliff. It also mistakes live volume for evaluation material — years of completed assessments are available as historical cases.
distractors.B: A defensible criterion for a routine high-volume process, but here it measures the wrong thing. Time saved per assessment does not capture whether the organisation can still produce assessments at all once a specialist has left.
distractors.C: Promises full automation of a drafting step inside a regulator-approved safety process with two layers of expert scrutiny. Nobody will accept it, and committing to it in qualification sets an expectation the delivery cannot meet.

explanation.concept: Volume determines how the benefit is expressed and how acceptance can be measured, not whether a use case is worth doing. Where volume is low and consequence is high, expect capacity, consistency and knowledge retention as the value, historical cases as the evaluation set, and expert review rather than a statistical threshold as the gate.
explanation.tip: A stem that mentions a retiring expert is pointing at knowledge loss as the real driver. When annual volume is in the tens, discount any option whose criterion needs statistical power.

topic: Sequencing a portfolio by data readiness
stem: A rail operator's AI board holds four qualified use cases with roughly equal estimated annual benefit and equal stakeholder backing. Their data positions differ: the first uses an already-governed, documented, API-accessible incident database; the second needs a data set whose owner has agreed access in principle but which contains personal data requiring an assessment that has not started; the third needs data held only in a supplier's system under a contract silent on the operator's right to use it for automated processing; the fourth needs data that exists but has no owner and no documented schema. Capacity allows two this year and at least one must ship. Which pair, and on what principle?

options.text: The first and the second: sequence on whether a blocker has a named owner and a determinable completion date, not on how large the blocker appears.
The first and the fourth, on the grounds that an undocumented internal data set is the cheapest blocker to clear because no external party is involved.
The third and the first, because the supplier contract can be reopened at the next annual review and the pairing spreads risk across dependencies.
The second and the third, because both blockers are legal in nature and can be cleared by a single legal workstream running alongside the builds.

explanation.correct: With benefit and support held equal, the only discriminator left is the shape of each blocker. The first has none and satisfies the must-ship constraint. The second has a blocker of the best possible kind: a willing owner, an established process and a knowable end date, so it can be worked in parallel with the first delivery. The third depends on a counterparty's goodwill on a contractual point nobody has raised, and the fourth requires manufacturing ownership and a schema before work can even be scoped — both have blockers with no date attached.

distractors.B: Underestimates the fourth. Undocumented data with no owner means someone must first be persuaded to become accountable for it, then the schema reverse-engineered and its quality established; that sequence routinely takes longer than a scheduled assessment with a cooperative owner.
distractors.C: Places a delivery on a contract negotiation the operator does not control, timed to an annual review that may not fall within the year. A silent contract is also more likely to require an amendment than a clarification.
distractors.D: Grouping the two hardest positions because both involve lawyers ignores the difference between a defined internal assessment and an external contractual negotiation. It also breaches the must-ship constraint by leaving nothing deliverable early.

explanation.concept: When candidate value is comparable, sequence on data readiness, and grade blockers by whether they have an owner and a date rather than by their apparent size. A large, scheduled, internally owned obstacle is safer to plan around than a small one that depends on a third party's willingness.
explanation.tip: Portfolio items usually equalise benefit deliberately so that only the dependency structure differs. Rank each blocker by 'who owns it and when does it end', and treat 'nobody' or 'unknown' as the worst answer.

topic: Questions that establish tolerance for error
stem: Which TWO questions establish a use case's tolerance for error during discovery? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: What accuracy do comparable systems at other firms in this industry publicly report achieving?
What happens downstream when the output is wrong, and who or what detects the error?
Which model tier and context window size does the team intend to use for this task?
How quickly, and at what cost, can a wrong output be reversed once someone has acted on it?
How many labelled historical examples are available for building the evaluation set?

explanation.correct: Tolerance is a property of consequences, not of models, so both questions look downstream of the output. Asking what happens when it is wrong, and who catches it, establishes whether an existing control absorbs errors or whether the system is the last line of defence — which is what decides the required quality bar and the human-in-the-loop design. Asking how fast and how cheaply an error can be reversed sets the autonomy level, because an instantly correctable action tolerates far more error than one that leaves the organisation.

distractors.A: Benchmarking against other firms describes what has been achieved elsewhere, on different data and different definitions. It may inform whether a target is realistic; it says nothing about how much error this business can absorb.
distractors.C: A design decision that follows from the tolerance rather than establishing it. Choosing the tier first, then asking how much error is acceptable, inverts the order.
distractors.E: An evaluation-construction question. It determines how precisely tolerance can be measured, but the tolerance itself is set by consequence and would be the same whether ten examples or ten thousand existed.

explanation.concept: Derive error tolerance from consequence and recoverability: what the wrong output causes, who detects it, how long it takes to notice, and what undoing it costs. These four answers set the quality bar, the guardrails and the autonomy level far more reliably than any target imported from another organisation.
explanation.tip: Options that reference other organisations' benchmarks or the team's intended technology are usually distractors in requirements items. Tolerance questions always point downstream of the output.

topic: High-volume stable classification against unit economics
stem: A parcel carrier routes about 9 million inbound customer messages a year into six categories, against a 200ms routing budget. Discovery finds a labelled corpus of 400,000 historical messages, accumulated from agents correcting the current keyword router's mistakes, and that the six categories have been unchanged for four years. The operations director asks for Claude to perform the classification. What should discovery recommend?

options.text: Use the model for all nine million messages a year, since it handles nuanced and multi-intent enquiries better than a trained classifier would.
Use the model but classify overnight in large batches, so the unit cost falls sharply without changing the approach.
Train a small supervised classifier on the labelled corpus for the routine path, reserving the model for low-confidence cases and category drift.
Decline the request, since routing is already performed by the keyword router in production and the six categories are stable.

explanation.correct: Every precondition for supervised learning is present: a large labelled corpus produced as a by-product of operations, a fixed and stable label set, and a task with no reasoning depth. At nine million messages a year the per-call difference between a hosted classifier and a general model dominates the economics, and a small model comfortably meets a 200ms budget. The model still earns a role — adjudicating the low-confidence band, where the labelled corpus is thinnest, and reading residual traffic for categories the taxonomy is missing.

distractors.A: Argues capability where the binding constraints are cost and latency at volume, and the six-category taxonomy has been stable for four years, so there is little nuance for extra capability to exploit.
distractors.B: Batching contradicts the requirement. Inbound messages must be routed on arrival against a 200ms budget; deferring classification to an overnight run means nothing is routed when it arrives.
distractors.D: Ignores the evidence in the stem: the labelled corpus exists precisely because agents keep correcting the keyword router, which is direct measurement of how often it is wrong. There is a real problem to solve.

explanation.concept: At very high volume with a stable label set and an existing labelled corpus, a purpose-trained classifier usually wins on cost and latency, and the model's best role is at the boundaries — the low-confidence residual and detecting when the taxonomy no longer fits. Reserve general capability for where variation actually lives.
explanation.tip: Three details together point away from a general model: a large labelled corpus, a label set stable for years, and volume in the millions. When all three appear, expect a hybrid with a small classifier on the main path.

topic: Sponsor demands a demonstration instead of discovery
stem: A retail bank's head of wealth has seen a competitor's adviser assistant and instructs the architect to skip the analysis and show something working in two weeks. There is no problem statement, no baseline and no approved data access, though a small set of anonymised adviser documents is already cleared for internal experimentation. The architect has two weeks and one engineer. What is the best next step?

options.text: Decline the instruction and insist on completing problem statement, baseline and data access before any build activity begins.
Build the demo on one real adviser task with the cleared documents, capturing that task's baseline and the sponsor's reactions.
Build a demonstration on synthetic adviser data spanning as many tasks as possible, to show the breadth of what is achievable.
Deliver an annotated slide walkthrough of the intended system instead, which avoids the data-access question entirely for now.

explanation.correct: The instruction is not negotiable, so the question is what the two weeks buy. Pointing the demonstration at one real task with cleared documents turns it into a feasibility spike and an elicitation instrument at once: the sponsor's live reaction to concrete output tells you more about the acceptance bar than a workshop would, and the baseline for that single task is cheap to capture alongside. The programme emerges with a demo, a measured starting point and evidence about requirements, rather than with a demo alone.

distractors.A: Correct in principle and unusable in practice. Refusing the sponsor's first request costs the relationship the whole engagement depends on, when discovery outputs can in fact be produced inside the demo work.
distractors.C: Breadth on synthetic data creates the worst outcome: a polished impression of capability that has never touched a real document, followed by an expectation that production is weeks away. It also produces no baseline and no requirements evidence.
distractors.D: A deck does not satisfy someone who has watched a competitor's system work, and it generates no learning at all. Avoiding the data question also leaves the project's largest unknown untested for two more weeks.

explanation.concept: When a sponsor short-circuits discovery, do not fight the format — reshape the artefact. A narrow demonstration on real data doubles as a feasibility spike, a baseline opportunity and the most effective elicitation device available, because stakeholders specify requirements far more precisely when reacting to concrete output than when asked in the abstract.
explanation.tip: Options that refuse the sponsor's request outright are almost never right at this tier. Look for the one that satisfies the request while extracting the discovery output the request skipped.

topic: Surfacing an unwritten rule observed in shadowing
stem: Shadowing underwriting assistants at a specialty insurer, the architect notices every one of them opens the broker's previous three submissions before quoting. No procedure mentions this, and none of them mentioned it when asked to describe their process. Asked why, one says 'you get a feel for whether they are shopping it around.' How should this be handled?

options.text: Disregard it; behaviour that appears in no documented underwriting procedure cannot be recorded as a requirement in the discovery pack.
Record a requirement that the system always retrieve the broker's previous three submissions into context before it produces a quote.
Raise it with the underwriting manager as an undocumented practice that should be stopped in the interests of consistency across the team.
Treat it as evidence that an unstated input matters, and elicit what the assistants read there and what decision it changes.

explanation.correct: The observed action is a proxy for an information need nobody has articulated — something about broker behaviour across submissions that affects how the quote is priced or how much scrutiny it gets. Copying the action without understanding the need risks building the wrong thing, while ignoring it discards the most valuable elicitation finding of the week. The next move is narrow and cheap: sit with two assistants over specific past submissions and establish what they read and what changed as a result.

distractors.A: Undocumented behaviour performed consistently by every practitioner is the strongest possible evidence that the documentation is incomplete. Discarding it guarantees the system reproduces the written process rather than the real one.
distractors.B: Automates the observed action rather than the underlying need. Retrieving three prior submissions into every request adds context and cost without anyone knowing what should be extracted from them or how it should influence the output.
distractors.C: Treats a universal practice as deviance. Before anything is stopped, someone has to establish what it achieves — and on the evidence it is compensating for a signal the formal process does not provide.

explanation.concept: When observed behaviour is consistent but unexplained, the requirement is the information need behind it, not the action itself. Elicit what the practitioner extracts and what decision it changes; only then decide whether the system needs the same input, a derived signal, or nothing at all.
explanation.tip: Shadowing items hinge on the difference between copying an action and understanding its purpose. The option that automates exactly what was observed is nearly always the trap.

topic: Acceptance criteria distinguished from success criteria
stem: In a discovery pack, what distinguishes acceptance criteria from success criteria?

options.text: Acceptance criteria are pass-or-fail tests applied before go-live; success criteria are outcomes measured once it is in use.
Acceptance criteria are technical measures owned by engineering; success criteria are financial measures owned by finance.
Acceptance criteria are drafted and proposed by the delivery team, while success criteria are proposed by the business sponsor.
Acceptance criteria apply during the pilot phase only; success criteria apply after the full production rollout has completed.

explanation.correct: The distinction is about what each one gates and when it is evaluated. Acceptance criteria are a gate: measured on a frozen evaluation set before release, they decide whether the thing built is the thing that was specified. Success criteria are an outcome: measured on live operation against a baseline, they decide whether building it was worth doing. A system can pass acceptance and fail success — that means the specification was wrong, which is a discovery failure rather than a delivery one.

distractors.B: Ownership by function is incidental and often wrong: acceptance criteria for a customer-facing assistant are usually business-owned, and success criteria frequently include operational rather than financial measures.
distractors.C: Both should be agreed jointly, and who drafts them is a working practice rather than a definition. The distinction survives regardless of who holds the pen.
distractors.D: Both apply at both stages. A production release has acceptance criteria of its own, and a pilot should have success criteria — otherwise nobody can say whether the pilot demonstrated anything.

explanation.concept: Acceptance answers 'did we build what we specified', measured before release on a fixed set. Success answers 'was the specification worth building', measured after release against a baseline. Keep them separate in the discovery pack, because they have different evaluators, different timing and different consequences when they fail.
explanation.tip: When two definitions are offered, sort by timing and by what each one gates. Options that separate them by function or by who wrote them are describing conventions, not definitions.

topic: Conditions required before promising unattended decisioning
stem: A local authority's revenues team wants an assistant to decide and issue single-person council tax discounts end to end, with no officer in the loop. Which THREE conditions must discovery establish before that commitment can responsibly be made? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: That a wrong decision can be identified and corrected within a defined window, and that it is clear who does so.
That the system outperforms the current revenues officers in every application category on a held-out set of cases.
That any duty to give reasons for the decision can be satisfied by output the system can actually produce.
That a named accountable officer owns the automated decisions and can be identified when a resident appeals.
That the assistant can be deployed on infrastructure sitting inside the authority's own data centre estate.

explanation.correct: Removing the human removes three things that the officer was silently providing, and each must be replaced explicitly. Error detection and correction ceases to be automatic, so a route and a window must be designed. The reasons given to the resident stop being written by a person, so the system must be capable of producing an explanation that meets whatever standard applies to the decision. And accountability cannot vanish with the officer: an appeal has to reach a named human who owns the decision. None of these is optional once the loop is opened.

distractors.B: Sets an unattainable and unnecessary bar. Category-by-category superiority is not what makes unattended operation safe; a system slightly below officer performance with fast detection and correction can be a better arrangement than a marginally better one with no recovery path.
distractors.E: A deployment topology choice driven by data protection and procurement policy. It may well be required for other reasons, but it has no bearing on whether decisions may be taken without a human, which is what the question asks.

explanation.concept: Before agreeing to unattended decisioning, enumerate what the human in the loop was providing beyond throughput: error detection, explanation, judgement on edge cases and accountability. Every function you remove must be explicitly re-provided somewhere in the design, or the loop was not closed — it was simply left open.
explanation.tip: For autonomy questions, ask what the removed human was doing that nobody listed in the requirements. Detection, reasons and accountability are the three that consistently go missing.

topic: A requirement stated as a solution
stem: A department head opens a discovery session by saying 'we need a chatbot on the intranet'. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Confirm the intranet as the channel and begin inventorying the site's content for indexing and chunking.
Explain that conversational interfaces are now a dated pattern, and propose a tool-using agent approach instead of a chatbot.
Work back to the problem: which question, asked by whom, how often, answered how today, and what an error costs.
Ask the department head to produce a written requirements document ahead of the next discovery session.

explanation.correct: A solution stated as a requirement hides the problem that motivated it, and the problem is what determines whether a conversational interface is even the right shape. Working back to who asks what, how often, and what a bad answer costs may reveal a search problem, a five-page policy nobody can find, a form that generates the questions, or a genuine assistant use case — and it produces the volume, baseline and consequence data the business case needs regardless of which it turns out to be.

distractors.A: Accepts the solution and starts building toward it. Content indexing is real work, but doing it before the question set is known risks indexing a corpus that does not contain the answers people actually need.
distractors.B: Substitutes the architect's preferred solution for the stakeholder's, which is the same error one level up. It also opens a technology argument with someone who has not yet been asked what they need.
distractors.D: Delegates the analysis back to the person least equipped to do it. Non-technical stakeholders asked for a requirements document typically return a more detailed description of the same solution.

explanation.concept: When a stakeholder states a solution, treat it as evidence about a problem rather than as a requirement. Work backwards to the decision, the actor, the frequency and the cost of error. The solution they named is useful information — it tells you how they imagine the fix — but it is not the thing to be specified.
explanation.tip: Stems that open with a technology noun rather than a problem are testing whether you will start designing. The correct move is always to recover the underlying decision and its cost.

topic: Raising the data access request in the first week
stem: Why should the formal data access request be raised in the first days of discovery rather than once the design has been agreed?

options.text: Requests are approved more readily when they are submitted before a specific design exists for reviewers to object to.
Approval runs on queues the team does not control, so it can proceed in parallel — and its outcome can invalidate the design.
The data owner must be recorded as a co-author of the requirements document for the eventual acceptance sign-off to be valid.
Access approvals lapse after a fixed period and must be re-submitted from scratch if they are obtained too early in the project.

explanation.correct: Access approval is almost always on the critical path and is the dependency the delivery team has the least influence over: it moves at the pace of another function's queue, its assessments and its meeting cycle. Starting it first means that elapsed time is spent while discovery continues rather than after it. The second reason is more important still — a refusal, or a condition such as redaction or a residency restriction, changes what can be designed, and learning that at the end wastes the whole phase.

distractors.A: The opposite is usually true: reviewers ask what the data will be used for, and a vague request without a described purpose tends to stall. Early submission works because of elapsed time, not because of ambiguity.
distractors.C: Data owners must be engaged and often become approvers, but co-authorship of requirements is not a validity condition for anything. This confuses a good working relationship with a governance rule.
distractors.D: Invents a general expiry rule. Some approvals are time-bounded and some are not; in either case the risk of starting early is trivial next to the risk of starting late.

explanation.concept: Start the longest externally controlled dependency first, and treat data access as both a schedule item and a design constraint. Approval conditions — redaction, retention limits, regional processing, purpose restriction — are requirements in their own right, and they must arrive before the design is fixed rather than after.
explanation.tip: Ask which dependency's clock the team cannot speed up. Those are the ones to start on day one, regardless of where they sit in the logical order of the work.

topic: Value case resting on an untested behaviour change
stem: A hospital group proposes Claude-generated plain-language discharge medication guidance, with the claimed benefit being fewer readmissions caused by medication errors. Discovery establishes that printed guidance already exists and is clinically accurate, that a recent audit found 62% of patients report not reading it, and that the proposed delivery is the same printed sheet with improved wording. What should discovery conclude about the value case?

options.text: The value case holds: clearer, plain-language wording will increase the share of patients who read the discharge sheet and act on it.
The value case fails, because readmission rates are influenced by too many clinical factors to be attributed to any single intervention.
The benefit needs a behaviour change the current channel fails to produce, so test delivery before treating wording as the constraint.
Commission a health-literacy specialist to rewrite the guidance once, since a one-off content improvement does not require a system at all.

explanation.correct: The audit has already located the failure: nearly two thirds of patients do not read the sheet, and the existing content is clinically sound. Improving wording addresses the quality of something people are not consuming, so the causal chain from output to outcome breaks at the delivery step, not the content step. The cheap and decisive discovery move is to test the channel — guidance delivered at a different moment, in a different medium, or with a spoken handover — because if that shifts readership, the content work becomes valuable, and if it does not, no rewrite will help.

distractors.A: Assumes the reason for non-readership is difficulty, which the audit does not establish. Patients also fail to read because of timing, discharge stress, format and the absence of any prompt to engage — none of which better wording addresses.
distractors.B: Overstates the attribution problem. Medication-error readmissions are identifiable and can be studied; the flaw in the value case is a broken causal step, not the impossibility of measurement.
distractors.D: Reaches the right scepticism about needing a system, but lands on the same broken assumption: a specialist rewrite is still content improvement delivered through the channel that 62% of patients ignore.

explanation.concept: Trace every value claim through its full causal chain to the outcome, and find the weakest link before designing. Where the benefit requires a behaviour change, check whether the current channel already produces that behaviour. If it does not, the constraint is delivery, and improving the artefact cannot move the outcome.
explanation.tip: When a stem gives you an adoption or readership statistic, it is naming the broken link. Any option that improves the artefact without touching how it reaches people is a distractor.

topic: Signals that a workshop has the wrong participants
stem: An architect is thirty minutes into a discovery workshop at a media company on rights-clearance checking. Which TWO observations most strongly indicate that the wrong people are in the room? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Participants disagree with one another about which rights categories are hardest to clear and why.
Participants ask the architect what comparable media companies have already implemented elsewhere.
Every description of how a case is handled is prefaced with 'I think what they usually do is…'.
Participants raise obscure clearance edge cases from memory that the architect had not considered.
Asked to pull up five recently cleared items, nobody present has access to the clearance system.

explanation.correct: Both are direct evidence that the participants are describing someone else's work. Reported speech — 'I think what they do' — marks second-hand knowledge, and second-hand accounts systematically omit exceptions, because the exceptions are exactly what does not get relayed upward. Lack of access to the operational system is the harder signal: people who perform the task have credentials for the system that records it, so its absence tells you the practitioners are elsewhere in the building.

distractors.A: Disagreement among people who do the work is informative rather than disqualifying. It usually reveals genuine variation between case types or between individuals, which is a finding worth chasing rather than a reason to change the invitation list.
distractors.B: A reasonable question from engaged participants, and a signal about their expectations rather than their proximity to the work. Answering it briefly and returning to their cases costs little.
distractors.D: The clearest sign that the right people are present. Unprompted edge cases come from operational memory and are among the most valuable things a workshop can produce.

explanation.concept: Judge a workshop's composition by the evidence participants can produce, not their titles. People who do the work speak in the first person, cite specific recent cases, and can open the system in front of you. Reported speech and lack of system access mean you are eliciting a description of the process rather than the process itself.
explanation.tip: The 'can you show me five recent cases' request is a fast composition test, and stems often include it for that reason. Inability to comply is the signal, not any answer given.

stem: A stakeholder states that the system 'must be explainable'. What must be established first to turn that into a testable requirement?

options.text: Whether the model can be configured to expose its intermediate reasoning tokens to the caller.
Whether a smaller model tier would be inherently more interpretable to reviewers than a larger one.
Whether the provider publishes interpretability research and documentation for the model in use.
Who needs the explanation, at what moment, and what action they will take on the basis of it.

explanation.correct: Explainability is not a property of a model in isolation; it is a relation between an output and a reader with a purpose. A caseworker overriding a recommendation needs the specific evidence the recommendation rested on. A customer contesting an outcome needs the reasons in terms they can act on. An auditor reviewing a sample two years later needs the inputs and the version that produced it. These imply completely different artefacts, and until you know which one is wanted, no requirement can be written and nothing can be tested.

distractors.A: Exposed intermediate reasoning is one possible mechanism, and often the wrong one — it is verbose, not addressed to the reader, and rarely suitable to show a customer. Choosing the mechanism before identifying the audience puts the answer before the question.
distractors.B: Model size does not determine whether a business explanation is adequate, and swapping tiers on interpretability grounds trades away capability for a property nobody has yet defined.
distractors.C: Vendor documentation describes the model, not the explanation a particular reader needs at a particular moment. It cannot substitute for a stated requirement.

explanation.concept: Resolve 'explainable' into audience, moment and consequent action before designing anything. Each combination produces a different artefact — evidence citations, a reason statement, an audit record — with different acceptance tests. The word alone is not a requirement, and neither is any mechanism chosen before the reader is known.
explanation.tip: Treat abstract quality words — explainable, transparent, robust, fair — as prompts to ask who, when and what will they do with it. The answer is never a model setting.

topic: Discovery uncovers an existing system covering most of the request
stem: A pharmaceutical company's medical affairs team asks for an assistant to answer questions about internal study protocols. In week two the architect discovers that another division built a Claude-based protocol question-answering system eight months ago; it is in production with about forty users, and its corpus covers roughly 70% of the documents medical affairs named. The remaining 30% sits in a different repository. The two teams have never spoken. What is the best next step?

options.text: Bring the two teams together, run medical affairs' real questions against the existing system, and scope the gap as the delivery.
Proceed with a separate build, since the existing system was designed around a different division's questions, needs and corpus.
Recommend that medical affairs adopt the existing system as it stands, with no corpus extension, and close the request.
Escalate the duplication to the group AI governance board and pause both efforts pending a formal consolidation review by architecture.

explanation.correct: Seventy percent corpus overlap plus a production system with real users is a substantial asset, but overlap is not the same as sufficiency — the value of a protocol assistant may sit entirely in the missing 30%. Running medical affairs' actual questions against the existing system settles that empirically in days and converts the engagement from a build into an extension with a much smaller footprint. It also creates the cross-division relationship that stops the next duplicate appearing.

distractors.B: Rebuilds retrieval, evaluation and operations that already exist and are running, and leaves the organisation maintaining two systems over an overlapping corpus. Divisional difference is a reason to test fit, not a reason to skip testing it.
distractors.C: Closes the request on a coverage assumption nobody has tested. If the questions medical affairs cares about depend on the missing repository, adoption fails immediately and the team's confidence in the programme goes with it.
distractors.D: Escalates before establishing the facts and pauses a production system serving forty users, which penalises the division that delivered. Governance visibility is worth having, but as an outcome of the assessment rather than a substitute for it.

explanation.concept: Before scoping a build, search for what already exists and test it against the new requirement empirically. Partial coverage usually converts a new system into an extension, which is faster, cheaper and reduces the estate. The test is always the requesting team's real questions, never the corpus overlap percentage on its own.
explanation.tip: A coverage figure below 100% in a stem is there to stop you choosing 'just use the existing one'. The answer sits between building fresh and adopting unchanged.

topic: Correcting a value case built on a miscoded volume figure
stem: A travel company's business case for a Claude rebooking assistant assumes 120,000 disruption contacts a year, taken from the contact centre's 'disruption' call-reason code. Discovery samples 300 of those calls: 44% are general itinerary questions miscoded by agents at wrap-up, and a further 9% are genuine disruptions on bookings made through a third party the company cannot rebook. What should the architect do with the value case?

options.text: Proceed as planned; the 44% miscoding rate will fall once contact-centre agents are retrained on call-reason coding as part of the rollout.
Proceed, but apply a flat 20% reduction to the projected benefit as a general prudence adjustment to the business case.
Re-derive addressable volume from the sample — about 47%, roughly 56,000 contacts — and restate the business case on that figure.
Discard the value case; systematically miscoded contact-reason codes make any volume estimate for this population unusable.

explanation.correct: The sample is the best evidence available and it is decisive: after removing miscoded contacts and third-party bookings the assistant cannot act on, roughly 47% of the coded population remains, which is about 56,000 contacts rather than 120,000. Three hundred cases support that share to within a few percentage points, so the corrected figure should be presented as a range rather than a point. Carrying the correction to the sponsor before approval is the part that matters — a benefit halved at discovery is a good decision, while the same discovery after go-live is a failed programme.

distractors.A: Agent retraining might improve future coding but cannot repair a historical basis, and it does nothing about the third-party bookings, which are structurally outside the assistant's reach whatever code is applied to them.
distractors.B: An arbitrary haircut discards the measurement that was actually taken. The sample supports a specific correction of roughly half; substituting a conventional adjustment understates the problem and leaves the sponsor unaware of it.
distractors.D: Over-corrects. The sample is exactly how a contaminated population gets estimated, and 300 cases give a usable figure with quantified uncertainty. Abandoning the estimate throws away the discovery finding.

explanation.concept: Validate the volume assumption underneath every value case by sampling the population the figure came from. Operational reason codes are entered under time pressure and are routinely wrong; the addressable subset is what the case should rest on, stated with the uncertainty its sample size supports.
explanation.tip: Whenever a business case cites a volume drawn from a category code, expect the item to test whether you sample it. Do the subtraction from the given percentages and check which option matches the arithmetic.

topic: Purposes of a de-scoping decision log
stem: Discovery records every item cut from scope together with the reason for the cut and the condition under which it would be reconsidered. Which TWO purposes does that log serve? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: It discharges the internal audit requirement for documented change control over the delivery baseline agreed at the gate.
It stops the same cut item being re-argued at every steering meeting, because the recorded condition decides its return.
It supplies the evaluation set for the descoped functionality at the point that functionality is eventually built.
It allows the delivery team to price each descoped item as a chargeable change request later in the engagement.
It preserves why a cut was made, so a later team does not reinstate scope whose original blocker is still in place.

explanation.correct: Both purposes concern the durability of a decision. Recording the reopening condition converts a recurring argument into a test — the item returns when the legal opinion arrives or the data set is cleared, not when someone raises it for the fourth time — which protects the plan without appearing obstructive. Recording the reason protects the next team, who will see an obvious gap in scope, assume it was an oversight, and reinstate work that is still blocked for exactly the reason nobody wrote down.

distractors.A: Change control governs modifications to an agreed baseline during delivery. Discovery-stage scope decisions precede that baseline, and no general audit rule requires them to be logged, even though logging them is good practice.
distractors.C: A record of what was cut and why contains none of the cases, inputs or expected outputs an evaluation set requires. Conflating the two would leave the eventual build with no test material.
distractors.D: A commercial use some engagements make of the artefact, but not a reason to keep it. The log's value is identical in an internal team with no billing relationship at all.

explanation.concept: Record scope cuts with their reason and their reopening condition. The reason survives the people who made the decision; the condition converts repeated lobbying into an objective trigger. Together they are what stops a descoped programme from silently re-expanding to its original size.
explanation.tip: For artefact-purpose items, ask what goes wrong if the artefact does not exist. Consequences that involve future people misreading the past are usually the keyed ones.

topic: First build selection under a board mandate for controlled adoption
stem: A regional health insurer can fund one of two qualified use cases. The first summarises provider contract terms for the network team: moderate measurable benefit, no member-facing output, no health data, an existing review workflow and a named owner. The second drafts member responses explaining claim denials: larger benefit, but member-facing, involving health data, subject to a regulator's requirements on how adverse decisions are explained, and the compliance function has not yet been engaged. The insurer has no Claude system in production, and its board has asked for evidence of controlled adoption before approving further investment. Which should be funded, and why?

options.text: The denial-response case, because the larger benefit justifies the additional controls and produces a far stronger narrative for the board at the next investment review.
The contract-summary case: the first build should establish the operating model on a low-exposure case while the denial case's compliance path runs in parallel.
The denial-response case, descoped so the assistant drafts only the factual sections of the letter while a person writes the explanation of the decision.
Fund both at half the requested budget, so the organisation gains delivery experience across two different risk profiles at once, within the same board window.

explanation.correct: Two facts in the stem decide it: nothing is in production, and the board has explicitly asked for evidence of controlled adoption rather than for maximum benefit. A first build has to produce an operating model — evaluation practice, review workflow, monitoring, incident handling — and it produces that far more reliably on a case with no member exposure, no health data and an owner already in place. The denial case is not abandoned: engaging compliance and establishing the explanation requirements is exactly the parallel work that makes it the credible second build.

distractors.A: Reads the board's request as being about size of benefit when it is about demonstrated control. A first-ever system that is member-facing, handles health data and touches regulated adverse-decision explanations is the least likely to produce the evidence the board asked for.
distractors.C: A thoughtful reduction, but it still places the organisation's first build in its highest-exposure area with compliance unengaged, and the split it proposes is fragile — the factual sections of a denial letter are precisely what the explanation is constructed from.
distractors.D: Halving the funding of two use cases in an organisation with no delivery experience risks completing neither within the board's evidence window, and it doubles the governance surface at the moment the programme can least afford an incident.

explanation.concept: Sequence the first production system for the evidence it must generate, not for the benefit it captures. Where an organisation has no operating experience, the initial build should exercise the full lifecycle on a low-exposure case; regulatory and compliance groundwork for the higher-value case proceeds in parallel and becomes the gate for the second build.
explanation.tip: When a stem states what a board or steering group has explicitly asked for, that request is the selection criterion. Options optimising for benefit against a stated mandate for control are distractors.
